title: Nature Doesn’t Know It’s Called Biology
author: Think Forward Educators
summary: The author confesses to having long believed that science was not their subject, and recognises this as the same limiting self-categorisation teachers challenge in students. The piece argues that the split into biology, chemistry and physics is a feature of school timetables and not of nature, tracing science back through natural philosophy and the Enlightenment. Drawing on Edward O. Wilson's idea of consilience, it holds that disciplines are different lenses on one world and that schools sometimes forget this. The central claim is that science is humanity's collective memory of what it has learned, and that schools owe every child an inheritance of that knowledge before asking them to extend it. The author distinguishes science, which asks what patterns have been observed and tested, from philosophy, which begins with ideals about how learning ought to occur. The closing argument is that science deserves a more central place in the curriculum because every child already lives inside the systems it explains.
points: School subject boundaries are an organising convenience, and treating them as real divisions in nature breeds the 'I'm not a science person' belief in adults and children alike.
Science is best understood as accumulated knowledge, a collective memory that every child is entitled to inherit before being asked to extend it.
The Science of Reading, Learning and Behaviour are bodies of tested evidence, which makes them different in kind from educational philosophies that start from ideals.
Because a child is at once a biological, chemical, physical and social being, teachers benefit from knowing something about all of those layers.
Giving science a central curriculum place is justified by the fact that all pupils live inside the systems it explains, not by the number who will become scientists.
quotes: Science, however, sat somewhere in the background. I admired people who knew it well, but I had convinced myself that it belonged to someone else.
We categorise ourselves into subjects we enjoy and subjects we don’t, rarely stopping to question whether those categories actually exist anywhere outside school.
The concept of Consilience argues that reality itself has never been divided. Only our study of it has.

Science is not merely a way of asking questions; it is humanity’s collective memory of the answers we have discovered so far. Schools have the responsibility of ensuring every child inherits that memory before asking them to extend it.
Philosophies often begin with ideals about how learning ought to occur. Science begins by asking what actually happens when human beings learn.

A child is simultaneously a biological organism, a chemical system, a physical body and a social being. Therefore, to understand our students, we need to understand something about all of those things.
Not because every child will become a scientist, but because every child is already living inside the systems science seeks to explain.
context: The author admits to the same limiting self-labelling that teachers criticise in students.
School subject categories are human constructs that do not exist in nature itself.
Disciplines are lenses on one reality, so their divisions are artefacts of study.
Science is accumulated knowledge that schools must hand on before asking pupils to extend it.
Evidence-based science differs from philosophy in starting from observed learning rather than ideals.
Understanding pupils fully requires knowledge across biology, chemistry, physics and the social sciences.
The case for central science is universal exposure, not producing future scientists.
